newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka boosts thermal power as rains fail anew.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka boosts thermal power as rains fail anew.

text.p: Sri Lanka's state-run electricity utility said on Thursday it was urgently increasing thermal power generation to ride out a drought caused by the failure of monsoon rains for the second straight year.

"We're confident that with new thermal power plants coming onstream we can ride out a possible drought and avoid power cuts which dislocated commerce and industry last year," said Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) chairman Arjun Deraniyagala.
"The northeast monsoon, which should have broken by the end of 1996, has failed," he told a news conference. "We have taken action to supply uninterrupted power throughout the year."
The Indian Ocean island endured daily power cuts of up to eight hours at the height of the drought last year.

Water levels in hydroelectric power reservoirs, which supply 85 percent of the country's electricity, have fallen to dangerously low levels with the failure of the northeast monsoon and the delayed onset of the southwest monsoon.

The CEB would cut dependence on hydropower to 57 percent of the total requirement by building more thermal power plants by June 1997, Deraniyagala said. The island now has an installed capacity of 1,135 megawatts of hydropower and 250 megawatts of thermal power.

Under emergency power generation measures, the CEB will buy 83 megawatts from small private sector diesel plants, he said. A 20-megawatt plant has been connected to the national grid and a 40-megawatt plant will be connected by April.
The CEB plans to install a 115-megawatt gas turbine and a 40-megawatt diesel plant by June to ensure enough power through the dry spell in the first half of 1998, Deraniyagala said.
In 1998, the CEB will add up to 108 megawatts by connecting three more diesel plants to the grid, enough to meet demand without any power cuts during that year, he said.
Future plans call for the CEB to commission a 100-megawatt combined cycle plant by 1999. A 50-megawatt diesel plant and a 150-combined cycle plant will be commissioned by 2000, he said.

A 70-megawatt hydropower plant will be commissioned by 2000 while a feasibility study is underway for a 300-megawatt coal power plant to be connected to the grid by 2003, ensuring a reliable supply of power over the next five years, he said.
The CEB had based its thermal power needs on very conservative rainfall estimates for 1997, Deraniyagala said.

"The northeast monsoon, which should have topped up our reservoirs at the end of last year, was not enough," he said. "But because of the corrective steps we have taken, the water storage is better than in early 1996."
Water levels in reservoirs were now sufficient to generate 800 million units of electricity compared to the 600 million units of storage capacity at the begining of 1996, he said.

Deraniyagala also said the CEB had no immediate plans to raise electricity tariffs for consumers, but could be forced to do so later if the cost of increased thermal power generation proved too much for the utility to bear.

"We're confident that as things are, the consumer need not be inconvenienced in any way," he said. "But consumers should also conserve power as much as possible because in future, we'll have to depend more on thermal power, which is extremely expensive."
